connector: Chapter 14 ended with nineteen trips and more than three hundred people led north. In Chapter 15, Harriet’s name spreads far past Maryland. As you read, notice the words Sterling chooses for Harriet, and the words other people use about her.

a.raw: harriet spoke more boldly than anyone expected the crowd cheered louder after every story
a.fixed: Harriet spoke more boldly than anyone expected. The crowd cheered louder after every story.
a.why: Capital H on Harriet; a period ends the first sentence; capital T starts the second. More boldly and louder are comparative adverbs: they compare how things were done.

b.raw: the crowd pushed harder than the police harriet held on more tightly than ever
b.fixed: The crowd pushed harder than the police. Harriet held on more tightly than ever.
b.why: Capital T starts the sentence; a period ends the first sentence; capital H on Harriet. Harder takes -er; more tightly uses more with an -ly adverb.

fill1.h1: An elevator lifts you up to a higher floor. Which root means lift?
fill1.why: lev means lift: e + lev + ate = lift up.

fill2.h1: A lever is a bar you push down to lift something heavy. Which root means lift?
fill2.why: lev means lift: lev + er = a tool for lifting.

fill3.h1: When you stand against something and won’t give in, which root means stand?
fill3.why: sist means stand: re + sist = stand against.

fill4.h1: To keep standing through hard times and never quit. Which root means stand?
fill4.why: sist means stand: per + sist = stand through, keep going.

notes.wgrd: An author’s feelings show in her word choice. Collect the words Sterling uses for Harriet. Is each one plain or admiring? Say how Sterling wants you to feel, and point to the word that told you.
vocab: To lift up; to raise to a higher level.
To stand against; to refuse to give in.
To keep going; to refuse to stop.
A person who worked to end (abolish) slavery.
notes.wordParts: lev means “lift” and sist means “stand”: elevate, lever, resist, persist.
notes.grammar: A comparative adverb compares two actions: faster, more carefully. Short adverbs usually take -er. Most -ly adverbs take more.
notes.spelling: In a long word, one syllable gets the stress and is said loud and clear. A vowel in a quiet syllable often fades to a lazy “uh,” the schwa: ab·o·LI·tion. To spell it, find a related word where that syllable is stressed: a·BOL·ish.

wordgame.voice: Tap a root, then the word it finishes. Or drag the root onto the word. Ask what each word is about: lifting, or standing?

why.t: At the end of Chapter 16, in the camp outside Beaufort, a woman pieces together an American flag from scraps of old clothing and says, “Our time is coming.” lev means lift, and sist means stand. Each right word sews one patch. Four each lesson, until the quilt is finished.

wordgame.winDay: Four more patches are sewn in. The next lesson’s words add more.
wordgame.win: The quilt is finished, and a North Star is stitched across its middle. lev = lift, sist = stand.

transcripts.welcome: Hey, it’s Marcus. Harriet has led more than three hundred people north, and now her name is spreading far past Maryland. Chapter 15 is called The Most of a Man. That’s something a famous man wrote about her. Today’s question: how does Sterling want you to see Harriet, and how can you tell?
transcripts.read: As you read, listen to the words. Sterling never says, I admire her. She shows it in the words she picks. Watch a fight on the streets of Troy, a long talk over a map in Canada, and a song soldiers sing as they march off to war. Write down Sterling’s words for Harriet.
transcripts.morphology: Two new roots. Lev means lift. Think of an elevator lifting you up. Sist means stand. When you resist, you stand against something. Every word today is lifting or standing. Ask which one, then sew the patch.

virtue.title: Seen at last
virtue.intro: In Chapter 15, Harriet speaks at meetings across the North and helps a crowd free Charles Nalle in Troy. John Brown calls her General Tubman. To the slaveowners she is “deluded”; to the abolitionists she is “the greatest heroine of the age.”
virtue.line: Write one sentence: Why does it matter who sees Harriet clearly?
